The hT-PT-LFIAs can be used for the multiplex detection of viral antigens (Influenza A/B, SARS-CoV-2), small molecule drugs (morphine, methamphetamine, ketamine) and nucleic acids (HPV 16/18), demonstrating versatility across various LFIA formats, good clinical performance in training cohort, and high repeatability for small molecule assay. By seamlessly integrating micro-engineering, nanotechnology, and smartphone-based sensing, this work provides a low-cost, portable, and broadly applicable PT-LFIAs detection strategy that bridges a critical technological gap.

title: Enhanced electrochemically-directed oligonucleotide synthesis via porous silica thin-film for DNA data storage
abstract: DNA-based data storage has emerged as a promising alternative for long-term information archiving and its implementation accelerates the development for on-chip large scale oligonucleotide synthesis. Among various technological routes, electrochemically directed synthesis offers exceptional synthesis-site density thanks to its compatibility with semiconductor microfabrication processes. Yet increasing density typically comes at the expense of reduced per-site oligonucleotide yield, compromising the practical utility of these synthesis platforms for reliable data recovery. Here we report a porous silica thin-film strategy in order to address this fundamental trade-off by substantially increasing the effective on-chip synthesis surface area while preserving spatial confinement during electrochemically generated acid-mediated deblocking. The porous thin-film, fabricated via a sacrificial templating approach, forms an interconnected high-surface-area porous network that enables efficient reagent transport and stable electrochemical control. The presented method enables an areal oligonucleotide yield of more than 1821 pmol/cm², which represents more than 11-fold enhancement compared to a planar silica substrate. Moreover, this platform achieves comparable error statistics of deletion, insertion and substitution compared to other laboratory-built DNA data writing systems. Using this platform, we demonstrated parallel synthesis of 121-nt oligonucleotides and successful encoding, writing and error-corrected recovery of digital information. These results establish a scalable strategy for high-yield on-chip DNA synthesis and provide a practical pathway towards integrated molecular data storage systems.

title: Scalable low-thermal-budget fabrication of suspended silicon nanowire devices
abstract: Silicon nanowires (Si NWs) are versatile one-dimensional building blocks for gas and biochemical sensors, MEMS/NEMS physical transduction platforms, and integrated electronic devices because of their high surface-to-volume ratios and compatibility with semiconductor processing. A key limitation of conventional top-down fabrication is its reliance on furnace-based high-temperature steps, such as thermal oxidation and LPCVD, which can induce residual stress and constrain post-CMOS integration because of thermal-budget limits above 400 °C. Here, we present a furnace-free, low-thermal-budget fabrication approach for suspended Si NWs with a maximum process temperature of 180 °C. The process forms suspended Si NWs at the top surface of both bulk Si substrates and SOI substrates with a 2 µm device layer. The method defines a nanoscale Si surface protrusion and uses a conformal Cr sidewall coating to preserve linewidth during DRIE release. The process yields suspended Si NWs with critical dimensions down to 50 nm, aspect ratios of up to 100, and array pitches of 5 µm, while supporting integration into junctionless field-effect transistor architectures. Electrical measurements confirm ohmic behavior in two-terminal NW devices and demonstrate depletion-mode current modulation in side-gated junctionless FETs, with a threshold voltage of 24 V and approximately 40× current modulation. After nominal 2 nm Pd functionalization, single-NW devices exhibit repeatable 1% H 2 sensing, producing near-complete current suppression of the p-type NW channel at sub-10 nW operating power. By eliminating furnace-based processing, the approach supports post-CMOS-compatible integration, avoids high-temperature stress-inducing process steps, and establishes a scalable platform for suspended Si NW devices.

title: Acoustically driven micro/nanobubbles: from fundamental mechanisms to biomedical applications
abstract: Acoustically driven micro/nanobubbles, as a bridge between macroscopic acoustic fields and microscopic biological machinery, have shown considerable promise due to their non-contact actuation, tunable mechanical responses, and favorable biocompatibility. Recent advances in bubble formulation and acoustic control have further expanded their capabilities, enabling targeted membrane permeabilization, enhanced molecular transport, and precise manipulation at the microscale. In this review, we summarize the fundamental mechanisms linking bubble dynamics to biologically relevant effects under ultrasound and establish quantitative design criteria that govern the coupling between acoustic parameters, bubble behavior, and therapeutic performance. We then organize biomedical applications across scales, spanning single-cell manipulation, tissue-level barrier modulation, and organ-scale imaging and therapeutic interventions. Particular attention is given to how acoustic modes and bubble configurations translate into measurable performance metrics, as well as the limitations that constrain reproducibility and safety in complex biological environments. Finally, we discuss key challenges for practical translation from an engineering perspective and propose strategies for improving controllability, standardization, and system integration. By providing a framework to overcome the inherent randomness of bubble-acoustic interactions in clinical translation, this review outlines a roadmap toward reliable and programmable mechano-bio platforms for closed-loop, patient-adaptive interventions.

title: Reconfigurable acoustic tweezers based on a programmable droplet array
abstract: Conventional acoustic manipulation relies on either direct acoustic radiation force acting on particles or indirect methods using acoustic streaming generated by acoustic pressure fields to manipulate particles. While acoustic devices generating standing waves can create patterned arrangements of particles and cells, these methods are typically limited to producing regular arrays in static configurations. This study introduces a dynamic acoustic field modulation method to overcome these limitations, significantly enhancing manipulation flexibility. Crucially, the propagation of acoustic energy varies substantially at liquid-solid interfaces or gas-solid interfaces due to differences in acoustic impedance matching. To exploit this, we use a digital microfluidic chip (DMF) to manipulate droplets and generate a programmable droplet array via the electrowetting-on-dielectric effect. By utilizing the programmable droplet array, we dynamically alter the spatial distribution of the acoustic field from a bulk acoustic wave (BAW) device in real time and demonstrate this technique's capability for capturing and manipulating particles on demand. We believe this is a unique method to create acoustic tweezers with great flexibility and reconfigurability, which holds promising potential for advanced applications in micromanipulation, micro-assembly, and beyond.

title: Magnetized joystick with dual-anisotropy for high-capacity wearable human-machine interactions
abstract: One of the urgent demands for flexible and wearable sensors is to achieve single-channel, less-sensor, and multi-output for effective communications. However, expansion of signal capacity on a single interface often requires sensor arrays, which significantly increases the complexity in electrode layout and multiple device design. In this work, we developed a flexible magnetized joystick (FMJ) with structurally induced eigenfrequency anisotropy by applying laser cutting process to a raw magnetized cubic. Using an eigenfrequency-polarity dual-anisotropy addressing method, we show that single FMJ can achieve four identifiable outputs based on the direction of in-plane mechanical inputs. According to the cantilever beam model, the eigenfrequency library can be expanded by adjusting cutting parameters, dimensions, and material properties, laying the foundation for further expanding signal capacity through the combination of multiple FMJs. The advantages of FMJs in terms of high capacity and multi-functionality are demonstrated through a range of human-machine interaction (HMI) applications, including game control, PowerPoint slides, robot car control, and a fingertip calculator. The increased signal requirement would not impose the complexity of electrical connection thanks to the interference-free parallel design of the electrodes. We expect that the development strategy will provide valuable insights for further advancement of high-capacity wearable HMI.

title: Curvature-driven passive mixing in three-dimensional conical helix micromixers
abstract: Passive microfluidic mixing is fundamentally constrained by the dominance of laminar flow, a limitation commonly addressed using embedded obstacles or surface modifications, often at the cost of increased fabrication complexity and hydraulic resistance. Here, we introduce a conical helix micromixer (CHM) that combines circular and helical microchannel topologies into a monolithic geometry capable of passively generating progressively intensified Dean vortices through continuously varying curvature. This curvature-driven mechanism induces strong transverse transport and achieves a mixing index (MI) > 95% in the first turn of the CHM across varying flow rates (1–2500 µL min −1 ) without requiring any internal roughness structures or external energy inputs, as validated by field-based mixing simulations. A central methodological contribution is a reduced-order planar representation of the full three-dimensional (3D) CHM geometry for flow-field analysis and optimization. Direct geometrical validation against the original 3D conical-helix centreline demonstrated projection-induced deviations below 2% across all investigated configurations, with most cases remaining below 1%, confirming that the planar representation preserves the dominant geometric characteristics of the true 3D flow path with negligible loss of fidelity. This reduced-order strategy lowered computational costs by approximately an order of magnitude, while preserving a strong correlation with full 3D field-based calculations across the investigated ranges of Reynolds numbers. Geometric and flow parameters were systematically explored using a Taguchi framework, while gradient-boosted machine-learning models were employed as mechanistic analytical tools to quantify parameter sensitivity. Both analyses consistently identified the inlet curvature radius as the dominant design variable governing Dean vortex onset and mixing-length compression, with tighter curvature significantly accelerating the development of transverse mixing. The results prove that controlled curvature modulation alone can function as an efficient passive mixing engine, providing a compact, fabrication-ready platform for microreactor synthesis, point-of-care diagnostics, and scalable lab-on-a-chip applications.

title: Monolithically integrated four-channel optoelectronic wind sensor with a mushroom-shaped sensitive structure
abstract: This paper presents a novel wind sensor based on a monolithically integrated four-channel optoelectronic chip and a mushroom-shaped sensitive structure. The four-channel optoelectronic chip consists of a centrally positioned light-emitting diode (LED) surrounded by four symmetrically arranged photodetectors (PDs). By employing monolithic integrated manufacturing technology, the consistency among the four PDs is significantly enhanced, thereby ensuring the overall symmetry of the sensor. In addition, an environmentally robust mushroom-shaped wind-sensitive structure is designed to interact with airflow while packaging the optoelectronic chip, providing reliable protection against outdoor environmental conditions. The manufactured sensor is subsequently installed in a wind tunnel for a series of measurements. The results demonstrate the capability of the sensor to monitor wind speeds ranging from 0 to 18 m/s and wind direction from 0 to 360°. This innovative design paves the way for advancements in wind-sensing devices, positioning it as a promising candidate for practical applications across various fields.

title: A fabrication-aware vectorized generative representation for topology optimization of path-defined MEMS microstructures
abstract: This work proposes a vectorized generative representation for fabrication-aware heuristic topology optimization of path-defined MEMS microstructures, addressing the trade-off between topological freedom and fabrication feasibility in MEMS inverse design. Pixel-level topology descriptions provide high design freedom and often require additional constraints to suppress disconnected or fabrication-incompatible layouts. Meanwhile, heuristic algorithms are attractive for non-gradient MEMS optimization, yet their efficiency depends critically on the compactness and validity of the design representation. The proposed representation addresses this limitation by mapping low-dimensional continuous design variables into connected, fabrication-compatible physical layouts, with topology evolution, boundary compatibility, linewidth modulation, spacing constraints, and geometric smoothing embedded directly into the generation process. This formulation provides a compact continuous search space in which path topology, spatial deployment, and local linewidth can be jointly explored while the prescribed fabrication constraints are maintained during decoding. Each generated layout is exported as a vector geometry for finite-element electrothermal labeling and rasterized as a morphology image for surrogate-model training, enabling rapid performance prediction during optimization. In a resistive thermal MEMS microheater used as the primary experimental validation case, infrared thermography showed that the measured temperature coefficient of variation decreased from 4.04% to 1.22%, while the ±2 °C effective isothermal area ratio increased from 34.7% to 95.6%. Finite-element results from a compliant micro-spring case demonstrated transferability: in-plane displacement increased by 30.6%, while peak von Mises stress decreased by 16.3% under matched footprint and loading. These results demonstrate the applicability of the proposed representation as a fabrication-compatible optimization interface for path-defined MEMS microstructures under distinct physical objectives.

title: Microcapillary-assisted acoustoelectric platform for selective single-cell isolation and in situ transfection
abstract: Abstract Single-cell transfection technologies hold tremendous promise for precision cell and immunotherapies. However, monolithic integration of cell isolation with targeted intracellular delivery remains technically challenging, especially within complex biological matrices. Herein, we present a microcapillary-assisted acoustoelectric single-cell selective isolation and sonoporative transfection platform (μC-ASSIST), which seamlessly sequences microcapillary-assisted dielectrophoresis (μC-DEP) for deterministic single-cell trapping with high-frequency surface acoustic waves (SAWs) for transient membrane poration within a unified workflow. We demonstrate the label-free, high-efficiency extraction of human non-small cell lung cancer (A549) cells from a complex white blood cell (WBC) background with a capture efficiency of 95%. Furthermore, we validate the highly efficient, contact-free intracellular delivery of diverse cargoes ranging from small dyes (PI) to functional small interfering RNA (siRNA) and large plasmid DNA (mRFP-C3), maintaining a high cell viability of 83.7% alongside a 78.1% transfection efficiency. Crucially, the targeted delivery of siBcl-xL significantly suppressed target mRNA expression and profoundly inhibited tumor cell motility. By circumventing off-target effects and cumbersome manual handling, the μC-ASSIST platform establishes a highly versatile, streamlined paradigm for precision single-cell engineering, holding immense potential for advancing functional genomics and next-generation gene therapies.

title: Towards advanced motion control systems for micro-scale magnetic drillers inside viscoelastic media
abstract: Microrobotic systems have the potential to reach regions of the body with significantly less invasiveness than conventional surgical tools. However, control over clinically relevant workspaces remains challenging due to limitations in magnetic field and robotic trajectory control. Here, we present a planar eight-solenoid magnetic field generator (MFG) that enables programmable velocity and heading of a 250 × 250 × 1250 µm 3 microscale driller through continuous field reorientation within a workspace of 20 × 20 × 20 cm 3 . The microscale driller achieved velocities up to 155 µm/s in 0.6 weight percent agarose gel, which mimics the mechanical properties of brain tissue, and executed turns beyond 90° with angular errors below 3°. These results demonstrate a scalable platform for precise and remote control of magnetically embedded microdevices, and support future development of minimally invasive systems for applications such as targeted therapeutic delivery and microsurgery.

title: Focusing and weighing microanalytes in liquid enabled by higher-order piezoelectric resonant membranes
abstract: Micro-electromechanical-system (MEMS) resonators have been recognized as powerful tools for precision mass detection. However, achieving both flexible on-chip capture of microanalytes and high-sensitivity liquid-phase sensing remains a technical challenge. We present a fully anchored multi-modal piezoelectric resonant membrane (PRM) that utilizes self-excited bulk acoustic waves to rapidly enrich sparsely dispersed microparticles within milliliter droplets and precisely locate them at the region of highest vibrational amplitude - the most sensitive area for resonance detection. The design of higher-order resonance modes preserves acoustofluidic enrichment performance while enabling reconfigurable particle distribution patterns through modulation of the acoustic field distribution. Experimental results demonstrate that the resonant frequency shift induced by the same mass load increases with the mode order, indicating that the sensing sensitivity is proportional to the resonance order. We systematically characterized the acoustofluidic parameters and electrical measurement performance of transverse modes from (0, 0) to (4, 0). This work shows that extending the integrated actuation-and-sense approach to consider multiple modes of resonances presents a toolbox for designing such miniaturized platforms to address nanogram-level mass analysis in liquid phase.

title: From footsteps to wireless events: infrastructure-native battery-free interfaces for human–environment interactions
abstract: Future intelligent environments require infrastructure-native interfaces that can sense human activities and directly generate wireless communication events using standard protocols. Achieving this remains challenging because human footsteps are transient, irregular, and often low-force, whereas standard wireless protocols such as Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) require substantial energy consumption. In this work, we present a self-powered floor interface that addresses this challenge through coordinated material, structural, and circuit design. The system integrates a high-performance PMN–PZT ceramic with a piezoelectric charge constant of d 33 = 962 pC/N for efficient energy transduction, a carefully engineered metallic substrate for enhanced stress transfer and recoverability, a threshold-regulated energy management circuit that regulates transient outputs into a usable burst-power window, and an ultra-low-power BLE interface for protocol-compatible transmission. With a 4.7 μF storage capacitor, the circuit provides 22.84 μJ of releasable energy, exceeding the approximately 17 μJ required for BLE cold start. Despite a footprint of only 30 mm, sub-millimeter thickness, and a prototype-level unit cost below $5, the system enables direct wireless triggering from a light actuation of approximately 12 N. Across 100 footstep trials involving 10 participants, the system achieved an average of 2.39 BLE packets per actuation, with up to 4 packets generated per event, and successfully delivered at least one wireless transmission in 97% of the trials. The proposed system directly translates irregular footsteps into reliable protocol-compatible wireless events and enables infrastructure-integrated human-environment interactions, including smart-home control, indoor localization, digital-twin interaction, and transportation-safety alerting. These results establish a practical route toward compact infrastructure-native battery-free interaction systems for future intelligent environments.

title: A review of ring-type rotational MEMS traveling-wave ultrasonic micromotors: design, detection, control, and application validation
abstract: The ring-type rotational microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) traveling-wave ultrasonic micromotor has emerged as an important candidate for micro- and small-scale precision rotary actuation because of its thin-film structure, low driving voltage, less electromagnetic interference, and strong potential for system-level integration. In recent years, continuous advances in MEMS wafer processing, lead zirconate titanate (PZT) thin-film deposition and etching, and multi-layer interconnect packaging have driven substantial progress in micro-stator design, output performance, online sensing, motion control, and application validation of ring-type rotational MEMS traveling-wave ultrasonic micromotors (R-MTWUMs). Centered on the framework of design, detection, control, and application, this review systematically summarizes the development of R-MTWUMs. It first outlines their operating principles and representative fabrication processes, and then critically reviews the evolution of micro-stator configurations from substrate supported structures to nodal circle anchored and flexibly supported structures, and further to stator teeth and ball-amplified structures. Key performance metrics, including quality factor, driving voltage, torque, and rotation speed, are comparatively analyzed. On this basis, the review further summarizes the main detection methods used for R-MTWUMs, discusses recent progress in angular position sensing, driving and control, feedback electrode-based mode monitoring, and closed-loop control, and assesses their application potential through the application validation. Finally, this review summarizes major development trends, discusses the remaining challenges in fabrication, mechanism, evaluation, on-chip sensing, and closed-loop control, and outlines future research directions to accelerate the transition of R-MTWUMs from laboratory prototypes to practical engineering systems.

title: Black-hole system: in vivo continuous bioligand-assisted elimination of circulating tumor cells to prevent cancer recurrence and metastasis
abstract: In vivo continuous eradication of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) following chemotherapy represents a promising strategy to prevent cancer recurrence and metastasis, but remains a practical challenge. Here, we propose a bioligand-assisted in vivo therapy for dynamic check and hemo clearance of CTCs, termed the "Black-hole" system. Inspired by hemopurification, the Black-hole system integrates a peristaltic pump to maintain continuous blood flow, a functionalized microfluidic reservoir for CTCs sustained capture, and flexible tubing with needles for in vivo blood withdrawal and reinfusion. In this system, blood is drawn from the left carotid artery, passes through the microfluidic reservoir to selectively withhold CTCs, and is subsequently reinfused into the right jugular vein. Demonstration in a live tumor-bearing mouse model demonstrated the biosafety and efficacy of the system for single-pass, in vivo CTCs elimination. No significant morphological alterations were observed in major organs after the Black-hole system therapy. Notably, mice receiving the Black-hole therapy following paclitaxel chemotherapy exhibited a 50% survival rate, along with a 16.7% reduction in overall tumor recurrence. We expect the Black-hole system to become a safe and effective adjuvant therapy for postoperative cancer management.

title: Low-voltage, ultra-broadband wearable MEMS ultrasound: a frequency-merged, wafer-scale framework for continuous in vivo cardiovascular imaging and monitoring
abstract: Continuous, non-invasive monitoring of central hemodynamics is essential for advanced cardiovascular care. Although wearable ultrasound enables deep-tissue sensing, its widespread clinical adoption is limited by the inherent physical trade-off between driving voltage and acoustic bandwidth, alongside the challenges of scaling microelectronic ultrasound devices for medical imaging. Here, we report a wearable, 81.7% broadband piezoelectric micromachined ultrasonic transducer (pMUT) array driven at a low voltage of 5 Vp. To address these bottlenecks, this study introduces two parallel innovations. First, we introduce a novel frequency-merging design, quantified by an equivalent circuit model, to effectively decouple the voltage-bandwidth trade-off. Second, we provide a comprehensive framework directing a scalable silicon-on-insulator wafer-level fabrication process towards fully in vitro and in vivo experimental characterizations for medical imaging. Enabled by these advancements, in vitro characterization demonstrates 0.64 mm axial and 1.27 mm lateral resolutions while maintaining a penetration depth of up to 9 cm in wire phantoms. In vivo, the wearable patch achieves comparable high-fidelity B-mode and M-mode imaging of carotid, brachial, and radial arteries within 4 cm depth to commercial rigid probes. Crucially, the device enables continuous, stable hemodynamic monitoring under limited daily postural activities for up to 9 hours. Inter-subject validation confirms precise blood pressure measurements, with deviations of 2.2 mmHg compared to FDA-approved clinical monitors. Leveraging standard semiconductor batch manufacturing, this work addresses the technical mismatch between low-voltage wearable devices and high-performance ultrasound transduction, creating a feasible development path for highly integrated, mass-producible cardiovascular ultrasound systems-on-chip.

title: Microwell-based nDEP multifunctional microfluidic system for single-cell capture and analysis
abstract: Microfluidic systems have revolutionized biological and clinical analyses, offering precise control over fluid manipulation at a microscale. In recent years, significant advancements have been made by integrating these systems with lab-on-a-chip technologies and expanding their applicability in various biotechnological and diagnostic fields. This work presents the development of a multifunctional lab-on-a-chip device that combines microwell structures with negative dielectrophoresis (nDEP) to enable both single-cell capture and in situ single-cell analysis. The proposed device was first validated using commercially available polystyrene microparticles (beads) and human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293 cells. Impedance analysis and real-time fluorescence microscopy was used to confirm nDEP-mediated high-efficiency single-cell capture within the device's microwells. Finally, single-cell lysis was performed to demonstrate in situ analysis inside the microwells. One of the key advantages of nDEP is its ability to function effectively in physiological media, which typically has high conductivity to model in vivo conditions. nDEP is compatible with high-conductivity environments which allows for optimization across a range of biomedical and clinical studies. In summary, our device provides a platform for a low-cost, miniaturized, and automated single-cell analysis which can be adapted to numerous applications, such as single-cell sequencing, protein analysis, and electrophysiological studies.
